title: Virtual environments
game_role: The shared files are listed in the game's credits.
objective: Understand what a virtual environment is and why it's used, and get to know the venv commands
story: Two ships are moored side by side at the harbor. One carries fish, the other flowers. Imagine what would happen if their cargo got mixed up! Each ship has its own hold. Python projects on your computer are the same: every project should have its own package hold. This hold is called a **virtual environment**.

sections.title: The problem: version clashes
sections.body:
Say your game project wants `pygame 2.5` and an old project wants `pygame 2.1`. If your computer has one Python and one package box, both can't be installed at the same time. Update one and the other breaks.

A **virtual environment** gives every project its own separate package box. That way projects don't affect each other.

sections.title: Creating and activating
sections.body:
These commands are typed in the terminal, inside the project folder:

```
python -m venv .venv
```

Then you **activate** the environment:

```
# Windows
.venv\Scripts\activate

# macOS and Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
```

If you see `(.venv)` at the start of the terminal line, the environment is active. Now every package you install with `pip install` goes only into this project. To close it, type `deactivate`.

sections.title: Sharing the environment
sections.body:
The virtual environment folder is big and isn't shared with others. Instead we share the package list:

```
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

Your friend creates their own virtual environment and installs the same packages with `pip install -r requirements.txt`. The `.venv` folder is also added to the `.gitignore` file so it isn't shared.

sections.title: A similar trap in code
sections.body:
We can see why keeping environments apart matters in Python too. If you assign a list to another variable, **the same list** is shared:

```python
game = ["pygame"]
site = game          # the same box!
site.append("flask")
print(game)          # ['pygame', 'flask']
```

For a separate copy, write `site = game.copy()`. A virtual environment is like giving each project its own copy.

examples.title: The shared box trap
examples.code:
game = ["pygame"]
site = game
site.append("flask")
print("Game:", game)

game = ["pygame"]
site = game.copy()
site.append("flask")
print("Game:", game)
print("Site:", site)

examples.title: Let's imitate environments
examples.note: Different versions of the same package live happily in two projects.

examples.title: Build the commands
examples.code:
env = ".venv"
print("Create:", f"python -m venv {env}")
print("Windows:", f"{env}\\Scripts\\activate")
print("macOS/Linux:", f"source {env}/bin/activate")

tasks.title: Prepare the commands
tasks.prompt:
Build the commands to create a virtual environment called `env_name` and to activate it on macOS/Linux:

- `create_cmd`: `python -m venv .venv`
- `activate_cmd`: `source .venv/bin/activate`
tasks.solution:
env_name = ".venv"

create_cmd = f"python -m venv {env_name}"
activate_cmd = f"source {env_name}/bin/activate"

print(create_cmd)
print(activate_cmd)

tasks.title: A separate copy
tasks.prompt: The `site` list should be a **separate copy** of the `game` list. Adding `"flask"` to `site` must not change `game`.
tasks.starter:
game = ["pygame", "rich"]

site = game
site.append("flask")

print("Game:", game)
print("Site:", site)
tasks.solution:
game = ["pygame", "rich"]

site = game.copy()
site.append("flask")

print("Game:", game)
print("Site:", site)

tasks.title: Find the clash
tasks.prompt: Two projects may want different versions of the same packages. Put the names of the packages that are **in both** with different versions into the `conflicts` list, in alphabetical order.
hints: For each package in project_a, check whether it's in project_b.
If it is and the versions differ, add it to the list; finally sorted()

challenge.title: Install into an environment
challenge.prompt: The `install(envs, env, package, version)` function should install the package **only** into the given environment. If the environment doesn't exist, it should create an empty one first.
hints: If the environment is missing: if env not in envs: envs[env] = {}

project_task.title: Project layout
project_task.prompt: Before sharing our game, let's choose which files to share. From the `files` list, remove **the ones starting with `.venv/` and the ones ending with `.pyc`**, put the rest into the `shared` list in alphabetical order, and print each on its own line.
project_task.solution:
files = ["main.py", ".venv/bin/python", "requirements.txt", "piko/game.py", "piko/game.pyc", ".venv/lib/site.py"]

shared = sorted([f for f in files if not f.startswith(".venv/") and not f.endswith(".pyc")])

for f in shared:
    print(f)
hints: Use not ... and not ... inside the list comprehension.
